source.title: Unified Scaling Laws for Compressed Representations
source.authors: Andrei Panferov; Ista Alexandra; Volkova; Ionut-Vlad Modoranu; V. Egiazarian; Mher Safaryan; †. DanAlistarh

record.tranche_reason: Extends loss-scaling analysis to compressed representations, including quantized, sparse, hybrid, and vector-quantized Llama-style language models.
record.gate_note: The paper fits and evaluates scaling laws for compressed-model loss and reports validation-loss results, so these are included. The RBBM sparse-training comparisons are not included: they evaluate a proposed training heuristic rather than testing the loss-scaling claim. Results cited from other work are also excluded.
record.test_reason: The study trains Llama-style models (30M–200M, C4, 100 tokens/param) under sparse, quantized, hybrid and vector-quantized formats. It fits a Chinchilla-form loss law with an effective parameter count N·ρ(R) and reports fit quality. This bears on whether the power-law form carries over to compressed training (V5), and, in a narrow range, on V1. Most rows concern the capacity factor ρ, not the loss power law itself.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that a Chinchilla-form law with an effective parameter count N·ρ(R) fits training over sparse, quantized, hybrid and VQ formats. ρ is a simple function of the representation's Gaussian MSE and factorizes across compression types except at extreme compression. They also claim practical uses: comparing formats (FP4 gives no gain over INT4) and an improved sparse-training heuristic (RBBM). Their stated limits are Llama-style models on C4 at 100 tokens/param, and possible extra effects at ultra-low precision.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops and evaluates a scaling law for compressed representations rather than reproducing the original dense-model scaling experiments; it uses Llama-style models, C4, and compression-aware training.
record.method_sensitivity: Capacity behavior and fit quality vary with quantizer and fitting formulation; the paper also reports differing behavior for low-precision representations and notes larger factorization error at extreme 2-bit quantization.

fits_no_version.finding: The ranking of numerical formats by Gaussian MSE matches their ranking by C4 validation loss; FP4 (E2M1) brings no gain over INT4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation Gaussian-MSE predicts the pretraining loss penalty of a compressed numerical format.

fits_no_version.finding: Representation capacity factorizes multiplicatively across combined compressions, with error around 1e-2 except at 2-bit precision.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effective-parameter multipliers of compression methods compose multiplicatively.

fits_no_version.finding: Quantizer choice sets a capacity ceiling (LSQ below 1, QuEST reaching 1), and the choice of ρ functional form changes fit error from 4.2e-4 to 1.1e-3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effective-parameter capacity of compressed training depends on the training algorithm and on the capacity parametrization.

record.problems: The evidence is restricted to decoder-only Llama-style models trained on C4 at 100 tokens per parameter, with model sizes of 30M–200M. The study does not test several orders of magnitude, compute scaling, compute-optimal allocation, downstream predictability, or other modalities. Some validation-loss values are presented only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: RBBM, RigL, and pruning-schedule comparisons in Section 5.2 and Appendix F were left out because they evaluate sparse-training methods rather than the loss-scaling claim. The theoretical convergence analysis and cited results were also not recorded as empirical scaling-law outcomes.

untested.parts: Scaling with compute or tokens independently (tokens fixed at 100/param); the several-orders-of-magnitude range (only 30M–200M, under one order); reported exponents.
Architecture shape not varied at fixed N.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer; only compressed-format text pretraining is tested.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal split across setups or fitting methods; the functional-form ablations concern the capacity factor only.

missing.what: Loss-law fit errors by formulation: sparsity 5.7e-4 (Frantar), 4.2e-4 (decoupled), 4.7e-4 (ours); quantization 4.5e-3 (Kumar), 1.9e-3 (decoupled), 2.1e-3 (ours).
Fitted L(MSE) curves across 30M, 50M and 100M models for the tanh form.
Authors' caveat that the law may need specific fits at ultra-low precision and for small VQ codebooks.
Vector-quantization scaling fits, run on 30M and 50M models only, show sub-unit saturation.

record.verdict_notes: The study extends rather than tests the original law: the power-law form in N and D is adopted from Chinchilla, and the experiments vary the representation, not scale over orders of magnitude. Only r1 bears on a version. The record's V7 links are dropped because the functional-form and quantizer ablations concern the capacity factor, not exponents or compute-optimal allocation.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests parameter scaling in compressed text pretraining in a data-rich regime; it does not test scaling with compute, independently vary tokens while other quantities are not bottlenecks, or cover several orders of magnitude in model size.
Tests compressed representations in text pretraining only; it does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study compares fitting formulations and representation-specific behavior, but does not test whether fitted exponents or the compute-optimal parameter/token split vary with setup.

rows.subject: Llama-architecture decoder-only Transformers
rows.operation_detail: Fit loss as a function of effective parameter count and dataset size for compressed representations.

conditions.value: sparse, quantized, sparse-quantized, and other tested compressed formats

rows.measure: Held-out/pretraining loss scaling with parameter count and dataset size
rows.value: The proposed form is Loss(N,D) ∼ A · (N · ρ(R))−α + B · D−β + E; the paper reports that it gives a good fit across the tested compressed representations.
rows.note: The empirical setup uses a fixed data-rich ratio of 100 training tokens per parameter and sizes from 30M to 200M; this does not establish the full range stated in V1.
rows.check: The fit is reported as good across representations; scope limits belong in untested, not the state. The value should carry the Table 1 fit errors (4.7e-4 sparsity, 2.1e-3 quantization), which no row records. No exponents are reported, and the N range is 30M–200M at a fixed 100 tokens/param.

rows.subject: Llama-architecture decoder-only Transformers
rows.operation_detail: Compare Gaussian-MSE-based representation-capacity rankings with validation loss from training in different numerical formats.

conditions.value: floating-point and integer formats, including 4-, 6- and 8-bit examples

rows.measure: C4 validation loss by numerical format
rows.value: figure only; the text states that the ranking by Gaussian MSE directly correlates with actual C4 validation loss.
rows.note: The text describes the relationship, but the individual plotted loss values are not available in the supplied text.
rows.check: This row shows that GMSE ranking of numerical formats correlates with C4 validation loss. It is a format-comparison result about the capacity metric, not a test of power-law loss scaling. Move it to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Llama-architecture decoder-only Transformers
rows.operation_detail: Fit representation capacity as a function of Gaussian MSE for different quantization approaches.
rows.measure: Representation capacity ρ as a function of Gaussian MSE
rows.value: The paper reports a close alignment between the capacity fits and says the proposed formulation provides a significantly better fit than the compared quantization law.
rows.note: This is a fit to the capacity factor in the loss-scaling law, not a test of extrapolating loss to much larger runs.
rows.check: This is a fit of ρ as a function of GMSE, compared with Kumar et al.: the study's own capacity formulation against prior laws. It is not loss scaling in N, D or compute.

rows.subject: Llama-architecture decoder-only Transformers
rows.operation_detail: Compare the capacity behavior of LSQ and QuEST quantizers.
rows.baseline: QuEST reaches ρ = 1 for low quantization error
rows.value: LSQ has an efficiency limit strictly below 1; the text attributes this to bias in its gradient estimator.
rows.note: The paper identifies a representation/algorithm-dependent difference in the fitted capacity behavior.
rows.check: The LSQ vs QuEST saturation difference concerns quantizer capacity, not the fitted exponents or compute-optimal split named in V7. The baseline is the study's other method, not a control.

rows.subject: Llama-architecture decoder-only Transformers
rows.operation_detail: Test whether capacity factorizes across combined compression representations.

conditions.value: sparse weights and activations; sparse-quantized weights; combined weight sparsity, weight quantization, and activation quantization

rows.measure: Error in factorized predictions of representation capacity
rows.value: The factorized approximation has error of order 10−2 in the reported cases; the appendix reports an exception for extreme 2-bit quantization, where ρ ≲ 0.1 and the approximation error is larger.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 8 error bars denote ±1 standard deviation from the mean.
rows.note: Appendix B reports element-wise errors of order 10−3–10−2 in its summary, and notes larger error for extreme 2-bit quantization.
rows.check: Factorization of capacity across compression types is a property of ρ, not of the loss power law. It fits no version.

rows.subject: Llama-architecture decoder-only Transformers
rows.operation_detail: Fit the combined scaling law using a decoupled formulation.
rows.note: The table reports fitting error for the combined scaling law L(MSE).
rows.check: This is an ablation of the functional form for ρ (the study's method against alternatives). V7 concerns exponents and compute-optimal allocation varying with setup; this does not measure that.

rows.subject: Llama-architecture decoder-only Transformers
rows.operation_detail: Fit the combined scaling law using the tanh functional form.
rows.note: The authors adopt tanh as their default functional form.
rows.check: Same as r6: it reports the fit error of the study's own adopted tanh form.

rows.subject: Llama-architecture decoder-only Transformers
rows.operation_detail: Fit the combined scaling law using the logistic functional form.
rows.note: The fitting error differs across functional forms.
rows.check: Same as r6: a functional-form ablation for ρ.

rows.subject: Llama-architecture decoder-only Transformers
rows.operation_detail: Fit the combined scaling law using a constrained logistic functional form.
rows.note: The error is larger than for the other listed functional forms.
rows.check: Same as r6: a functional-form ablation for ρ.

relationships.condition: Compressed-format (sparse, quantized, sparse-quantized, VQ) pretraining of Llama-style models, 30M–200M, C4, 100 tokens/param
relationships.reason: A Chinchilla-form law with effective N·ρ(R) fits across representations, with fit errors 4.7e-4 (sparsity) and 2.1e-3 (quantization) per Table 1 (r1).
relationships.display_finding: A Chinchilla-form law using effective size N·ρ(R) fits the representations, with errors of 4.7e-4 for sparsity and 2.1e-3 for quantization.

relationships.condition: Ultra-low precision (2-bit, ternary) and VQ codebooks below 8 entries
relationships.reason: The authors state the law may need specific fits there, suggesting second-order effects. This rests on the Discussion text, not on a recorded row (r1).
relationships.display_finding: The authors suggested that 2-bit or ternary precision and codebooks below eight entries may require specific fits because of second-order effects.

relationships.condition: Dense and compressed Llama models, 30M–200M at fixed 100 tokens/param
relationships.reason: The power-law-in-N form, inherited from Chinchilla, fits with low error over this narrow range. The form is adopted rather than independently tested and no exponents are reported (r1).
relationships.display_finding: The adopted Chinchilla-derived parameter power law fitted losses with low error across the narrow 30M–200M parameter range.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
